entities.name: Metrodorus of Chios
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Metrodorus of Chios, an influential Greek philosopher of the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE, emerged from the intellectual ferment of Ionia to become a prominent figure within the Democritean school. His philosophical contributions, characterized by a radical skepticism concerning sensory perception and the ultimate nature of reality, positioned him as a crucial intellectual bridge between the atomic theory of Democritus and the later epistemological considerations of Pyrrhonism and Epicureanism. Flourishing in an era marked by intense philosophical debate following the Sophistic movement, Metrodorus challenged established notions of knowledge and certainty, advocating for a profound agnosticism regarding the divine and the cosmos.

His core philosophical contribution revolved around the assertion that 'no one knows anything, not even whether we know nothing or not.' This extreme skepticism extended to all forms of knowledge, including the very possibility of knowing, effectively predating and influencing the later Pyrrhonian tradition. Metrodorus adopted Democritus's atomic theory as a framework for understanding the physical world but departed significantly in his epistemological conclusions, arguing that while atoms and void constitute reality, human perception is inherently limited and unreliable. He famously posited that 'everything is a dream and nothing is true,' a statement reflecting his deep distrust of sensory experience and rational inference as paths to truth.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Metrodorus of Chios played a significant role in developing ancient skepticism, directly influencing Epicurean epistemology and contributing to the intellectual currents that shaped Hellenistic philosophy. His radical doubts about knowledge laid groundwork for later, more formal skeptical schools.
